{{Short description|Boundary condition for generalized functions}}
{{Confuse|trace-class operator}}
[[File:Trace_operator_illustration.png|right|thumb|A function defined on a rectangle (top figure, in red), and its trace (bottom figure, in red).]]
In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''trace operator''' extends the notion of the [[function restriction|restriction of a function]] to the boundary of its domain to "generalized" functions in a [[Sobolev space]]. This is particularly important for the study of [[partial differential equation]]s with prescribed boundary conditions ([[boundary value problem]]s), where [[weak solution]]s may not be regular enough to satisfy the boundary conditions in the classical sense of functions.

== Motivation ==
On a bounded, smooth [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]] <math display="inline">\Omega \subset \mathbb R^n</math>, consider the problem of solving [[Poisson's equation]] with inhomogeneous [[Dirichlet boundary conditions]]:

:<math>\begin{alignat}{2}
-\Delta u &= f &\quad&\text{in } \Omega,\\
u &= g &&\text{on } \partial \Omega
\end{alignat}</math>

with given functions <math display="inline">f</math> and <math display="inline">g</math> with regularity discussed in the [[Trace operator#Application|application section]] below. The weak solution <math display="inline">u \in H^1(\Omega)</math> of this equation must satisfy

:<math>\int_\Omega \nabla u \cdot \nabla \varphi \,\mathrm dx = \int_\Omega f \varphi \,\mathrm dx</math> for all <math display="inline">\varphi \in H^1_0(\Omega)</math>.

The <math display="inline">H^1(\Omega)</math>-regularity of <math display="inline">u</math> is sufficient for the well-definedness of this [[integral equation]]. It is not apparent, however, in which sense <math display="inline">u</math> can satisfy the boundary condition <math display="inline">u = g</math> on <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math>: by definition, <math display="inline">u \in H^1(\Omega) \subset L^2(\Omega)</math> is an [[equivalence class]] of functions which can have arbitrary values on <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math> since this is a null set with respect to the n-dimensional [[Lebesgue measure]].

If <math display="inline">\Omega \subset \mathbb R^1</math> there holds <math display="inline">H^1(\Omega) \hookrightarrow C^0(\bar \Omega)</math> by [[Sobolev inequality|Sobolev's embedding theorem]], such that <math display="inline">u</math> can satisfy the boundary condition in the classical sense, i.e. the restriction of <math display="inline">u</math> to <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math> agrees with the function <math display="inline">g</math> (more precisely: there exists a representative of <math display="inline">u</math> in <math display="inline">C(\bar \Omega)</math> with this property). For <math display="inline">\Omega \subset \mathbb R^n</math> with <math display="inline">n > 1</math> such an embedding does not exist and the trace operator <math display="inline">T</math> presented here must be used to give meaning to <math display="inline">u |_{\partial \Omega}</math>. Then <math display="inline">u \in H^1(\Omega)</math> with <math display="inline">T u = g</math> is called a weak solution to the boundary value problem if the integral equation above is satisfied. For the definition of the trace operator to be reasonable, there must hold <math display="inline">T u = u |_{\partial \Omega}</math> for sufficiently regular <math display="inline">u</math>.

== Trace theorem ==

The trace operator can be defined for functions in the [[Sobolev space|Sobolev spaces]] <math display="inline">W^{1,p}(\Omega)</math> with <math display="inline">1 \leq p < \infty</math>, see the section below for possible extensions of the trace to other spaces. Let <math display="inline">\Omega \subset \mathbb R^n</math> for <math display="inline">n \in \mathbb N</math> be a bounded domain with [[Lipschitz boundary]]. Then<ref name="Gagliardo1957" /> there exists a bounded linear '''trace operator'''
: <math>T\colon W^{1, p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial \Omega)</math>
such that <math display="inline">T</math> extends the classical trace, i.e.
: <math>T u = u |_{\partial \Omega}</math> for all <math display="inline">u \in W^{1, p}(\Omega) \cap C(\bar \Omega)</math>. 
The continuity of <math display="inline">T</math> implies that 
: <math>\| T u \|_{L^p(\partial \Omega)} \leq C \| u \|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}</math> for all <math display="inline">u \in W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math> 
with constant only depending on <math display="inline">p</math> and <math display="inline">\Omega</math>. The function <math display="inline">T u</math> is called trace of <math display="inline">u</math> and is often simply denoted by <math display="inline">u |_{\partial \Omega}</math>. Other common symbols for <math display="inline">T</math> include <math display="inline">tr</math> and <math display="inline">\gamma</math>.

=== Construction ===

This paragraph follows Evans,<ref name="Evans1998, traces" /> where more details can be found, and assumes that <math display="inline">\Omega</math> has a <math display="inline">C^1</math>-boundary.{{efn|name=c1boundary}} A proof (of a stronger version) of the trace theorem for Lipschitz domains can be found in Gagliardo.<ref name="Gagliardo1957" /> On a <math display="inline">C^1</math>-domain, the trace operator can be defined as [[continuous linear extension]] of the operator

: <math>T:C^\infty(\bar \Omega)\to L^p(\partial \Omega)</math>

to the space <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math>. By [[Dense set|density]] of <math display="inline">C^\infty(\bar \Omega)</math> in <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math> such an extension is possible if <math display="inline">T</math> is continuous with respect to the <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math>-norm. The proof of this, i.e. that there exists <math display="inline">C > 0</math> (depending on <math display="inline">\Omega</math> and <math display="inline">p</math>) such that

: <math>\|Tu\|_{L^{p}(\partial \Omega)}\le C \|u\|_{W^{1, p}(\Omega)}</math> for all <math>u \in C^\infty(\bar \Omega)</math>,

is the central ingredient in the construction of the trace operator. A local variant of this estimate for <math display="inline">C^1(\bar \Omega)</math>-functions is first proven for a locally flat boundary using the [[divergence theorem]]. By transformation, a general <math display="inline">C^1</math>-boundary can be locally straightened to reduce to this case, where the <math display="inline">C^1</math>-regularity of the transformation requires that the local estimate holds for <math display="inline">C^1(\bar \Omega)</math>-functions.

With this continuity of the trace operator in <math display="inline">C^\infty(\bar \Omega)</math> an extension to <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math> exists by abstract arguments and <math display="inline">Tu</math> for <math display="inline">u \in W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math> can be characterized as follows. Let <math display="inline">u_k \in C^\infty(\bar \Omega)</math> be a sequence approximating <math display="inline">u \in W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math> by density. By the proven continuity of <math display="inline">T</math> in <math display="inline">C^\infty(\bar \Omega)</math> the sequence <math display="inline">u_k |_{\partial \Omega}</math> is a [[Cauchy sequence]] in <math display="inline">L^p(\partial \Omega)</math> and <math display="inline">T u = \lim_{k \to \infty} u_k |_{\partial \Omega}</math> with limit taken in <math display="inline">L^p(\partial \Omega)</math>.

The extension property <math display="inline">T u = u |_{\partial \Omega}</math> holds for <math display="inline">u \in C^{\infty}(\bar \Omega)</math> by construction, but for any <math display="inline">u \in W^{1, p}(\Omega) \cap C(\bar \Omega)</math> there exists a sequence <math display="inline">u_k \in C^\infty(\bar \Omega)</math> which converges uniformly on <math display="inline">\bar \Omega</math> to <math display="inline">u</math>, verifying the extension property on the larger set <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega) \cap C(\bar \Omega)</math>.

{{notelist|refs=
{{efn|name=c1boundary|<math display=“inline”>C^k</math> boundary: We say <math display=“inline”>\partial U</math> is <math display=“inline”>C^k</math> if for each point <math display=“inline”>x^0 \in \partial U</math> there exist <math display=“inline”>r>0</math> and a <math display=“inline”>C^k</math> function <math display=“inline”>\gamma\colon\mathbb{R}^{n-1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> such that—upon relabeling and reorienting the coordinate axes if necessary—we have: 

<math display=“inline”>U\cap B(x^0,r)=\{x\in B(x^0,r)|x_n>\gamma (x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}) \}</math>}}
}}

=== The case p = ∞ ===

If <math display="inline">\Omega</math> is bounded and has a <math display="inline">C^1</math>-boundary then by [[Morrey's inequality]] there exists a continuous embedding <math display="inline">W^{1, \infty}(\Omega) \hookrightarrow C^{0, 1}(\Omega)</math>, where <math display="inline">C^{0, 1}(\Omega)</math> denotes the space of [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz continuous]] functions. In particular, any function <math display="inline">u \in W^{1, \infty}(\Omega)</math> has a classical trace <math display="inline">u |_{\partial \Omega} \in C(\partial \Omega)</math> and there holds

: <math>\| u |_{\partial \Omega} \|_{C(\partial \Omega)} \leq \| u \|_{C^{0, 1}(\Omega)} \leq C \| u \|_{W^{1, \infty}(\Omega)}.</math>

== Functions with trace zero ==

The Sobolev spaces <math display="inline">W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)</math> for <math display="inline">1 \leq p < \infty</math> are defined as the [[Closure (topology)#Closure of a set|closure]] of the set of compactly supported test functions <math display="inline">C^\infty_c(\Omega)</math> with respect to the <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math>-norm. The following alternative characterization holds:

: <math>W^{1, p}_0(\Omega) = \{ u \in W^{1, p}(\Omega) \mid T u = 0 \} = \ker(T\colon W^{1, p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial \Omega)),</math>

where <math display="inline">\ker(T)</math> is the [[Kernel (linear algebra)|kernel]] of <math display="inline">T</math>, i.e. <math display="inline">W^{1, p}_0(\Omega)</math> is the subspace of functions in <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math> with trace zero.

== Image of the trace operator ==

=== For p > 1 ===

The trace operator is not surjective onto <math display="inline">L^p(\partial \Omega)</math> if <math display="inline">p > 1</math>, i.e. not every function in <math display="inline">L^p(\partial \Omega)</math> is the trace of a function in <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math>. As elaborated below the image consists of functions which satisfy an <math display="inline">L^p</math>-version of [[Hölder condition|Hölder continuity]].

==== Abstract characterization ====
An abstract characterization of the [[Image (mathematics)|image]] of <math display="inline">T</math> can be derived as follows. By the [[isomorphism theorems]] there holds

: <math>T(W^{1,p}(\Omega)) \cong W^{1, p}(\Omega) / \ker(T\colon W^{1, p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial \Omega)) = W^{1, p}(\Omega) / W^{1, p}_0(\Omega)</math>

where <math display="inline">X / N</math> denotes the [[Quotient space (linear algebra)|quotient space]] of the Banach space <math display="inline">X</math> by the subspace <math display="inline">N \subset X</math> and the last identity follows from the characterization of <math display="inline">W^{1, p}_0(\Omega)</math> from above. Equipping the quotient space with the quotient norm defined by

: <math>\|u\|_{W^{1, p}(\Omega) / W^{1, p}_0(\Omega)} = \inf_{u_0 \in W^{1, p}_0(\Omega)} \|u - u_0\|_{W^{1, p}(\Omega)}</math>

the trace operator <math display="inline">T</math> is then a surjective, bounded linear operator

: <math>T\colon W^{1, p}(\Omega) \to W^{1, p}(\Omega) / W^{1, p}_0(\Omega) </math>.

==== Characterization using Sobolev–Slobodeckij spaces ====

A more concrete representation of the image of <math display="inline">T</math> can be given using [[Sobolev space#Sobolev–Slobodeckij spaces|Sobolev-Slobodeckij spaces]] which generalize the concept of Hölder continuous functions to the <math display="inline">L^p</math>-setting. Since <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math> is a ''(n-1)''-dimensional Lipschitz [[Topological manifold|manifold]] embedded into <math display="inline">\mathbb R^n</math> an explicit characterization of these spaces is technically involved. For simplicity consider first a planar domain <math display="inline">\Omega' \subset \mathbb R^{n-1}</math>. For <math display="inline">v \in L^p(\Omega')</math> define the (possibly infinite) norm

: <math>\| v \|_{W^{1-1/p, p}(\Omega')} = \left( \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega')}^p + \int_{\Omega' \times \Omega'} \frac{ | v(x) - v(y) |^p }{|x - y|^{(1 - 1/p) p + (n-1)}}\,\mathrm d(x, y) \right)^{1/p} </math>
:
which generalizes the Hölder condition <math display="inline">| v(x) - v(y) | \leq C | x - y|^{1-1/p}</math>. Then

: <math>W^{1-1/p, p}(\Omega') = \left\{ v \in L^p(\Omega') \;\mid\; \| v \|_{W^{1-1/p, p}(\Omega')} < \infty \right\}</math>

equipped with the previous norm is a Banach space (a general definition of <math display="inline">W^{s,p}(\Omega')</math> for non-integer <math display="inline">s > 0</math> can be found in the article for [[Sobolev space#Sobolev–Slobodeckij spaces|Sobolev-Slobodeckij spaces]]). For the ''(n-1)''-dimensional Lipschitz manifold <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math> define <math display="inline">W^{1-1/p, p}(\partial \Omega)</math> by locally straightening <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math> and proceeding as in the definition of <math display="inline">W^{1-1/p, p}(\Omega')</math>.

The space <math display="inline">W^{1-1/p, p}(\partial \Omega)</math> can then be identified as the image of the trace operator and there holds<ref name="Gagliardo1957" /> that

: <math>T\colon W^{1, p}(\Omega) \to W^{1 - 1/p, p}(\partial \Omega)</math>

is a surjective, bounded linear operator.

=== For p = 1 ===

For <math display="inline">p = 1</math> the image of the trace operator is <math display="inline">L^1(\partial \Omega)</math> and there holds<ref name="Gagliardo1957" /> that

: <math>T\colon W^{1, 1}(\Omega) \to L^1(\partial \Omega)</math>

is a surjective, bounded linear operator.

== Right-inverse: trace extension operator ==

The trace operator is not injective since multiple functions in <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math> can have the same trace (or equivalently, <math display="inline">W^{1, p}_0(\Omega) \neq 0</math>). The trace operator has however a well-behaved right-inverse, which extends a function defined on the boundary to the whole domain. Specifically,  for <math display="inline">1 < p < \infty</math> there exists a bounded, linear '''trace extension operator'''<ref name="Necas1967" />

: <math>E\colon W^{1-1/p, p}(\partial \Omega) \to W^{1, p}(\Omega)</math>,

using the Sobolev-Slobodeckij characterization of the trace operator's image from the previous section, such that

: <math>T (E v) = v</math> for all <math display="inline">v \in W^{1-1/p, p}(\partial \Omega)</math>

and, by continuity, there exists <math display="inline">C > 0</math> with

: <math>\| E v \|_{W^{1, p}(\Omega)} \leq C \| v \|_{W^{1-1/p, p}(\partial \Omega)}</math>.

Notable is not the mere existence but the linearity and continuity of the right inverse. This trace extension operator must not be confused with the [[Sobolev space#Extension operators|whole-space extension operators]] <math display="inline">W^{1, p}(\Omega) \to W^{1, p}(\mathbb R^n)</math> which play a fundamental role in the theory of Sobolev spaces.

== Extension to other spaces ==

=== Higher derivatives ===

Many of the previous results can be extended to <math display="inline">W^{m, p}(\Omega)</math> with higher differentiability <math display="inline">m = 2, 3, \ldots</math> if the domain is sufficiently regular. Let <math display="inline">N</math> denote the exterior unit normal field on <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math>. 
Since <math display="inline">u |_{\partial \Omega}</math> can encode differentiability properties in tangential direction only the normal derivative <math display="inline">\partial_N u |_{\partial \Omega}</math> is of additional interest for the trace theory for <math display="inline">m = 2</math>. Similar arguments apply to higher-order derivatives for <math display="inline">m > 2</math>.

Let <math display="inline">1 < p < \infty</math> and <math display="inline">\Omega \subset \mathbb R^n</math> be a bounded domain with <math display="inline">C^{m, 1}</math>-boundary. Then<ref name="Necas1967" /> there exists a surjective, bounded linear '''higher-order trace operator'''

: <math>T_m\colon W^{m, p}(\Omega) \to \prod_{l = 0}^{m-1} W^{m-l-1/p,p}(\partial \Omega)</math>
:
with Sobolev-Slobodeckij spaces <math display="inline">W^{s, p}(\partial \Omega)</math> for non-integer <math display="inline">s > 0</math> defined on <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math> through transformation to the planar case <math display="inline">W^{s, p}(\Omega')</math> for <math display="inline">\Omega' \subset \mathbb R^{n-1}</math>, whose definition is elaborated in the article on [[Sobolev space#Sobolev–Slobodeckij spaces|Sobolev-Slobodeckij spaces]]. The operator <math display="inline">T_m</math> extends the classical normal traces in the sense that

: <math>T_m u = \left(u |_{\partial \Omega}, \partial_N u |_{\partial \Omega}, \ldots, \partial_N^{m-1} u |_{\partial \Omega}\right)</math> for all <math display="inline">u \in W^{m, p}(\Omega) \cap C^{m-1}(\bar \Omega).</math>

Furthermore, there exists a bounded, linear right-inverse of <math display="inline">T_m</math>, a '''higher-order trace extension operator'''<ref name="Necas1967" />

: <math>E_m\colon \prod_{l = 0}^{m-1} W^{m-l-1/p,p}(\partial \Omega) \to W^{m, p}(\Omega)</math>.

Finally, the spaces <math display="inline">W^{m, p}_0(\Omega)</math>, the completion of <math display="inline">C^\infty_c(\Omega)</math> in the <math display="inline">W^{m, p}(\Omega)</math>-norm, can be characterized as the kernel of <math display="inline">T_m</math>,<ref name="Necas1967" /> i.e.

: <math>W^{m, p}_0(\Omega) = \{ u \in W^{m, p}(\Omega) \mid T_m u = 0 \}</math>.

=== Less regular spaces ===

==== No trace in ''L<sup>p</sup>'' ====

There is no sensible extension of the concept of traces to <math display="inline">L^p(\Omega)</math> for <math display="inline">1 \leq p < \infty</math> since any bounded linear operator which extends the classical trace must be zero on the space of test functions <math display="inline">C^\infty_c(\Omega)</math>, which is a dense subset of <math display="inline">L^p(\Omega)</math>, implying that such an operator would be zero everywhere.

==== Generalized normal trace ====

Let <math display="inline">\operatorname{div} v</math> denote the distributional [[divergence]] of a [[vector field]] <math display="inline">v</math>. For <math display="inline">1 < p < \infty</math> and bounded Lipschitz domain <math display="inline">\Omega \subset \mathbb R^n</math> define

:<math>E_p(\Omega) = \{ v \in (L^p(\Omega))^n \mid \operatorname{div} v \in L^p(\Omega) \}</math>

which is a Banach space with norm

:<math>\| v \|_{E_p(\Omega)} = \left( \| v \|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p + \| \operatorname{div} v \|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p \right)^{1/p}</math>.

Let <math display="inline">N</math> denote the exterior unit normal field on <math display="inline">\partial \Omega</math>. Then<ref name="Sohr2001, normal traces" /> there exists a bounded linear operator

: <math>T_N\colon E_p(\Omega) \to (W^{1-1/q, q}(\partial \Omega))'</math>,

where <math display="inline">q = p / (p-1)</math> is the [[conjugate exponent]] to <math display="inline">p</math> and <math display="inline">X'</math> denotes the [[continuous dual space]] to a Banach space <math display="inline">X</math>, such that <math display="inline">T_N</math> extends the normal trace <math display="inline">(v \cdot N) |_{\partial \Omega}</math> for <math display="inline">v \in (C^\infty(\bar \Omega))^n</math> in the sense that

: <math>T_N v = \bigl\{ \varphi \in W^{1 - 1/q, q}(\partial \Omega) \mapsto \int_{\partial \Omega} \varphi v \cdot N \,\mathrm{d} S \bigr\}</math>.

The value of the normal trace operator <math display="inline">(T_N v)(\varphi)</math> for <math display="inline">\varphi \in W^{1-1/q,q}(\partial \Omega)</math> is defined by application of the [[divergence theorem]] to the vector field <math display="inline">w = E \varphi \, v</math> where <math display="inline">E</math> is the trace extension operator from above.

''Application.'' Any weak solution <math display="inline">u \in H^1(\Omega)</math> to <math display="inline">- \Delta u = f \in L^2(\Omega)</math> in a bounded Lipschitz domain <math display="inline">\Omega \subset \mathbb R^n</math> has a normal derivative in the sense of <math display="inline">T_N \nabla u \in (W^{1/2,2}(\partial \Omega))^*</math>. This follows as <math display="inline">\nabla u \in E_2(\Omega)</math> since <math display="inline">\nabla u \in L^2(\Omega)</math> and <math display="inline">\operatorname{div}(\nabla u) = \Delta u = - f \in L^2(\Omega)</math>. This result is notable since in Lipschitz domains in general <math display="inline">u \not\in H^2(\Omega)</math>, such that <math display="inline">\nabla u</math> may not lie in the domain of the trace operator <math display="inline">T</math>.

== Application ==

The theorems presented above allow a closer investigation of the boundary value problem

:<math>\begin{alignat}{2}
-\Delta u &= f &\quad&\text{in } \Omega,\\
u &= g &&\text{on } \partial \Omega
\end{alignat}</math>

on a Lipschitz domain <math display="inline">\Omega \subset \mathbb R^n</math> from the motivation. Since only the [[Hilbert space]] case <math display="inline">p = 2</math> is investigated here, the notation <math display="inline">H^1(\Omega)</math> is used to denote <math display="inline">W^{1,2}(\Omega)</math> etc. As stated in the motivation, a weak solution <math display="inline">u \in H^1(\Omega)</math> to this equation must satisfy <math display="inline">T u = g</math> and

:<math>\int_\Omega \nabla u \cdot \nabla \varphi \,\mathrm dx = \int_\Omega f \varphi \,\mathrm dx</math> for all <math display="inline">\varphi \in H^1_0(\Omega)</math>,

where the right-hand side must be interpreted for <math display="inline">f \in H^{-1}(\Omega) = (H^1_0(\Omega))'</math> as a duality product with the value <math display="inline">f(\varphi)</math>.

=== Existence and uniqueness of weak solutions ===

The characterization of the range of <math display="inline">T</math> implies that for <math display="inline">T u = g</math> to hold the regularity <math display="inline">g \in H^{1/2}(\partial \Omega)</math> is necessary. This regularity is also sufficient for the existence of a weak solution, which can be seen as follows. By the trace extension theorem there exists <math display="inline">Eg \in H^1(\Omega)</math> such that <math display="inline">T(Eg) = g</math>. Defining <math display="inline">u_0</math> by <math display="inline">u_0 = u - Eg</math> we have that <math display="inline">T u_0 = Tu - T(Eg) = 0</math> and thus <math display="inline">u_0 \in H^1_0(\Omega)</math> by the characterization of <math display="inline">H^1_0(\Omega)</math> as space of trace zero. The function <math display="inline">u_0 \in H^1_0(\Omega)</math> then satisfies the integral equation

:<math>\int_\Omega \nabla u_0 \cdot \nabla \varphi \,\mathrm dx = \int_\Omega \nabla (u - Eg) \cdot \nabla \varphi \, \mathrm dx = \int_\Omega f \varphi \,\mathrm dx - \int_\Omega \nabla Eg \cdot \nabla \varphi \,\mathrm dx</math> for all <math display="inline">\varphi \in H^1_0(\Omega)</math>.

Thus the problem with inhomogeneous boundary values for <math display="inline">u</math> could be reduced to a problem with homogeneous boundary values for <math display="inline">u_0</math>, a technique which can be applied to any [[linear differential equation]]. By the [[Riesz representation theorem]] there exists a unique solution <math display="inline">u_0</math> to this problem. By uniqueness of the decomposition <math display="inline">u = u_0 + Eg</math>, this is equivalent to the existence of a unique weak solution <math display="inline">u</math> to the inhomogeneous boundary value problem.

=== Continuous dependence on the data ===

It remains to investigate the dependence of <math display="inline">u</math> on <math display="inline">f</math> and <math display="inline">g</math>. Let <math display="inline">c_1, c_2, \ldots > 0</math> denote constants independent of <math display="inline">f</math> and <math display="inline">g</math>. By continuous dependence of <math display="inline">u_0</math> on the right-hand side of its integral equation, there holds

: <math>\| u_0 \|_{H^1_0(\Omega)} \leq c_1 \left( \|f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)} + \|Eg\|_{H^1(\Omega)} \right)</math>

and thus, using that <math display="inline">\| u_0 \|_{H^1(\Omega)} \leq c_2 \| u_0 \|_{H^1_0(\Omega)}</math> and <math display="inline">\| E g \|_{H^1(\Omega)} \leq c_3 \| g \|_{H^{1/2}(\Omega)}</math> by continuity of the trace extension operator, it follows that

: <math>\begin{align}\| u \|_{H^1(\Omega)} &\leq \| u_0 \|_{H^1(\Omega)} + \| Eg \|_{H^1(\Omega)} \leq c_1 c_2 \|f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)} + (c_3+c_1 c_2) \|Eg\|_{H^1(\Omega)} \\
	&\leq c_4 \left(\|f\|_{H^{-1}(\Omega)} + \|g\|_{H^{1/2}(\partial \Omega)} \right)\end{align}</math>

and the solution map

: <math>H^{-1}(\Omega) \times H^{1/2}(\partial \Omega) \ni (f, g) \mapsto u \in H^1(\Omega)</math>

is therefore continuous.
